title_en: Notice of the Supreme People's Court, the Supreme People's Procuratorate, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Public Security on Issuing the Standards for Identification of Severe Injuries (Trial Implementation)
full_text_en:
Supreme People's Court, Supreme People's Procuratorate, Ministry of Justice, and Ministry of Public Security

Notice on Issuing the Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (Trial)

Document No. (86) Si Fa Yan Zi No. 249

To the Judicial Departments (Bureaus), High People's Courts, People's Procuratorates, and Public Security Departments (Bureaus) of all provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities directly under the Central Government:

The "Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (Trial)" formulated by the Ministry of Justice are hereby issued to you as the standard for forensic medical examiners to assess serious injuries, and shall be applied with reference in forensic medical examinations. Any problems encountered during the two-year implementation period shall be reported promptly through the proper channels for further revision and improvement.

Appendix: Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (Trial)

August 15, 1986

Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries (Trial)

Chapter I General Provisions

Article 1 These identification standards are established in accordance with Article 85 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China, based on the theories and techniques of medicine and forensic medicine, and combined with the practical experience of forensic medical examinations in China, to provide a scientific basis for the identification of serious injuries.

Article 2 In assessing the degree of injury, the scientific principle of seeking truth from facts must be adhered to, and the specific injury circumstances shall be analyzed specifically.

At the time of identification, a comprehensive analysis and overall assessment shall be made based on the injury condition at the time of the injury and its consequences or outcomes.

The degree of injury includes the primary changes at the time of injury, serious complications directly related to the injury, and serious sequelae caused by the injury. When assessing, the original degree of injury shall not be reduced due to improvement from clinical treatment or a favorable prognosis, nor shall the original degree of injury be increased due to errors in medical treatment, aggravation of the original condition due to the injury, or individual specific constitution.

Article 3 The identification of the degree of injury shall be conducted by a forensic medical examiner or by a physician appointed or engaged by the judicial authority. When conducting the identification, the forensic medical examiner or physician has the right to understand the circumstances of the case related to the injury, access medical records, and inspect the scene.

Chapter II Disability of Limbs

Article 4 Disability of limbs refers to the loss of a limb or the loss of function of an intact limb due to various injurious factors.

Article 5 Loss of a limb refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Loss of any thumb;
(2) Loss of any three or more of the remaining four fingers, excluding the thumb;
(3) Loss of any two fingers of one hand and their metacarpal bones;
(4) Loss of fifty percent of one foot or fifty percent of the heel;
(5) Loss of all toes of one foot; etc.

Article 6 An intact limb with loss of function refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Ankylosis or deformity of the shoulder joint, or loss of joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(2) Flail shoulder joint;
(3) Restriction of elbow joint movement in extension, with range of motion less than 90 degrees, or in neutral position, with range of motion less than 10 degrees;
(4) Flail elbow joint;
(5) Humerus fracture complicated by pseudarthrosis or malunion affecting upper limb function;
(6) Malunion of forearm fracture with ankylosis in pronation or supination;
(7) Forearm fracture or soft tissue injury causing severe impairment of wrist, palm, or finger function, inability to oppose fingers or grasp objects(1);
(8) Ankylosis, flexion contracture deformity, wrist drop, or loss of wrist joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(9) Flail wrist joint;
(10) Metacarpal fracture severely affecting finger function, inability to oppose fingers or grasp objects;
(11) Thumb contracture deformity, inability to oppose fingers or grasp objects;
(12) Contracture deformity of the remaining four fingers excluding the thumb, inability to oppose fingers or grasp objects;
(13) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the hip joint, or loss of joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(14) Ankylosis, angular deformity, contracture deformity of the knee joint, or loss of joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(15) Ankylosis, contracture deformity of the ankle joint, or loss of joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(16) Femur or tibia/fibula fracture complicated by pseudarthrosis or malunion, with shortening exceeding 5 cm, angular deformity exceeding 30 degrees, or severe rotational deformity;
(17) Open fracture of long bones of the limbs, comminuted closed fracture complicated by sequelae such as osteomyelitis or nonunion;
(18) Scar contracture of limb soft tissue affecting major joint function, with loss of joint range of motion reaching fifty percent;
(19) Complete severance or defect of important nerves of the limb;
(20) Severance, thrombosis, or embolism of important blood vessels of the limb causing circulatory disturbance, severely affecting limb function;
(21) Crush injury of the limb causing crush syndrome; etc.

Chapter III Disfigurement of Appearance

Article 7 Disfigurement of appearance refers to damage to a person's face(2) resulting in deformation, ugliness, and functional impairment.

Article 8 Damage to the eye region refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Loss of one eyeball;
(2) Ptosis severely affecting vision;
(3) Injury to the eye region causing complete severance of the nasolacrimal duct, severance of the medial canthal ligament resulting in visual impairment and affecting facial appearance; etc.

Article 9 Damage to the auricle refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Loss of fifty percent or more of one auricle, or total loss of both auricles exceeding sixty percent of one ear;
(2) Injury to the auricle causing severe deformation; etc.

Article 10 Loss or severe collapse of the external nose causing deformation.

Article 11 Injury to the lips severely affecting facial appearance, speech, and eating.

Article 12 Injury to the zygomatic bone causing mouth opening less than 1 cm; malunion of zygomatic fracture with displacement causing severe facial deformation.

Article 13 Damage to the jaw and temporomandibular joint refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Fracture of the maxilla or mandible causing facial deformation;
(2) Loss or fracture of seven or more teeth affecting facial appearance, chewing, and speech;
(3) Injury to the temporomandibular joint causing mouth opening less than 1 cm; deviation of the healthy side of the mandible towards the injured side causing asymmetry of the lower face; etc.

Article 14 Other disfigurement of appearance refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Deep second-degree or higher burns or scalds on the face causing scar contracture, resulting in deformity of one of the areas such as the mouth, nose, eyelids, or auricle, leading to disfigurement and functional impairment;
(2) Scalp injury causing eyelid deformity, or auricle defect causing significant facial deformation;
(3) Hypertrophic scar remaining after facial injury, with area greater than 4 square centimeters; cord-like scar longer than 5 cm, causing disfigurement and functional impairment of the eyelids, nose, lips, cheeks, etc.;
(4) Facial nerve injury causing paralysis of most or all facial muscles;
(5) Extensive fine scars or extensive pigmentation remaining after facial injury causing facial ugliness;
(6) Deep second-degree or higher burns or scalds on the neck followed by scar contracture affecting neck movement and facial appearance; etc.

Chapter IV Loss of Hearing(3)

Article 15 After injury, hearing loss for speech in one ear at the level of 91 decibels or above.

Article 16 After injury, hearing loss for speech in both ears at the level of 60 decibels or above.

Chapter V Loss of Vision(4)

Article 17 Loss of vision due to various injuries refers to any of the following circumstances:

(1) Blindness in one eye after injury;
(2) Low vision in both eyes after injury, with one eye having low vision of grade 2.

Article 18 Injury to the eye region or craniocerebral injury causing visual field defect (diameter less than 10 degrees).

Chapter VI Injury to Other Organs and Loss of Function

Section 1 Craniocerebral Injury

Article 19 Scalp avulsion involving an area of twenty-five percent of the scalp; scalp injury causing loss of viability of an area reaching twenty-five percent of the scalp; scalp injury causing hemorrhagic shock.

Article 20 Linear fracture or depressed fracture of the skullcap accompanied by symptoms of brain parenchyma and vascular injury or compression of major blood vessels, and obvious neurological signs.

Article 21 Open craniocerebral injury, comminuted skull fracture, rupture of the dura mater, contusion and laceration of the brain, retention of foreign body in the cranial cavity.

Article 22 Basilar skull fracture accompanied by obvious symptoms such as cerebrospinal fluid leakage, internal ear hemorrhage, etc.

Article 23 Craniocerebral injury with immediate unconsciousness and occurrence of monoplegia, hemiplegia, aphasia, or other obvious neurological symptoms and signs.

Article 24 Craniocerebral injury causing epidural hematoma, subdural hematoma, or intracerebral hematoma.

Article 25 Craniocerebral injury causing intracranial infection such as meningitis, brain abscess, etc.

Article 26 Craniocerebral injury causing injury to cranial nerves other than the olfactory nerve that is difficult to recover.

Article 27 Traumatic epilepsy after craniocerebral injury.

Article 28 Various severe organic mental disorders after craniocerebral injury.

Article 29 Symptoms or syndromes caused by organic damage to the nervous system due to craniocerebral injury, such as traumatic carotid-cavernous sinus fistula, diabetes insipidus, diabetes mellitus, hypopituitarism syndrome, hypothalamic syndrome, etc.

Section 2 Neck Injury

Article 30 Injury to the laryngopharynx, trachea, neck, or floor of the mouth or adjacent tissues causing severe respiratory difficulty; cicatricial stenosis after trauma to the above parts causing respiratory difficulty.

Article 31 Injury to neck blood vessels causing hemorrhagic shock or respiratory difficulty; formation of carotid artery aneurysm or carotid-jugular fistula after neck injury.

Article 32 Thrombosis of one side of the common carotid artery or vertebral artery after neck injury.

Article 33 Neck injury involving the brachial plexus severely affecting upper limb function; neck injury involving the apex of the pleura causing pneumothorax.

Article 34 Thyroid gland injury accompanied by recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causing severe functional impairment.

Article 35 Injury to the thoracic duct.

Article 36 Injury to the pharynx or esophagus causing local abscess, mediastinitis, or pyosepticemia.

Article 37 Injury to the pharynx or esophagus causing stenosis with obstructive symptoms.

Article 38 Retention of deep foreign body after neck injury affecting the function of corresponding tissues or organs or having potential danger.

Article 39 Loss of voice that is difficult to recover or severe hoarseness after laryngeal injury.

Section 3 Chest Injury

Article 40 Rib fracture puncturing the lung causing hemorrhage or pneumothorax.

Article 41 Fracture of three or more ribs or multiple rib fractures causing respiratory difficulty.

Article 42 Sternal fracture causing respiratory difficulty, myocardial contusion, or cardiac tamponade affecting heart function; sternal fracture causing rupture of the trachea or bronchus; sternal fracture injuring intrathoracic blood vessels causing hemothorax.

Article 43 Chest injury causing extensive chest wall tissue defect or extensive scar deformity severely affecting respiration or other functions.

Article 44 Perforating chest injury causing pneumothorax, hemothorax, mediastinal emphysema, respiratory distress syndrome, rupture of trachea or bronchus, and retention of foreign body in the lung or thoracic cavity.

Article 45 Injury to the trachea or esophagus causing mediastinitis, mediastinal abscess, mediastinal emphysema, hemopneumothorax, or empyema.

Article 46 Heart injury or retention of foreign body in the heart.

Article 47 Injury to major thoracic blood vessels, traumatic aortic aneurysm, or traumatic chylothorax.

Article 48 Chest injury causing empyema, lung abscess, atelectasis, bronchopleural fistula, esophagopleural fistula, or bronchoesophageal fistula.

Article 49 Severe compression of the chest causing circulatory disturbance, respiratory dysfunction, or intracranial hemorrhage.

Article 50 Loss of one breast in a female; loss of lactation function due to injury to both breasts.

Section 4 Abdominal Injury

Article 51 Perforation or rupture of the stomach, intestines, or biliary system, or even without perforation causing hemorrhagic shock.

Article 52 Perforation or rupture of the liver, spleen, pancreas, or other organs, formation of abscess, aneurysm, or severe functional impairment due to the injury.

Article 53 Renal laceration or rupture with hemorrhage causing shock; urinary extravasation requiring surgical treatment (including renal artery embolization); late complication of renal injury such as renovascular hypertension or renal dysfunction.

Article 54 Injury to the ureter causing urinary extravasation or severe ureteral stricture leading to hydronephrosis.

Article 55 Abdominal injury causing peritonitis, pyosepticemia, intestinal obstruction, intestinal fistula, etc.

Article 56 Abdominal injury causing intra-abdominal hemorrhage or other conditions requiring laparotomy.

Section 5 Pelvic Injury

Article 57 Pelvic fracture causing rupture and hemorrhage of retroperitoneal large blood vessels leading to shock; causing rupture of the bladder, urethra, or other internal organs; causing severe narrowing of the birth canal affecting function.

Article 58 Rupture or severance of the urethra requiring surgical repair.

Article 59 Urethral stricture after urethral injury causing dysuria, urinary leakage through fistula, or renal dysfunction.

Article 60 Rupture of the bladder.

Article 61 Injury to the penis causing loss or severe deformity affecting function.

Article 62 Scrotal avulsion involving an area of sixty percent of the scrotal skin; loss of both testicles or injury to both testicles causing testicular atrophy or necrosis; occlusion of the spermatic duct affecting reproductive function.

Article 63 Injury to the external genitalia or vagina with hemorrhage causing shock.

Article 64 Rupture of the vagina involving surrounding organs, formation of fistula, or scar formation affecting function.

Article 65 Various injuries causing perforation or rupture of the uterus or adnexa; late complication of uterine or adnexal injury such as organ atrophy or affecting organ development.

Article 66 Injury to a pregnant woman causing premature labor, stillbirth, placental abruption, or miscarriage complicated by hemorrhagic shock or severe infection.

Article 67 Severe injury to the external genitalia of a young girl, or injury to the vagina.

Article 68 Injury to the anus causing severe fecal incontinence or severe anal stricture.

Section 6 Spinal and Spinal Cord Injury

Article 69 Fracture or dislocation of the spinal vertebrae accompanied by spinal cord injury or injury to multiple spinal nerve roots.

Article 70 Spinal cord injury affecting spinal cord function with residual sequelae, such as impaired limb movement function, defecation and urination disorders, and sexual dysfunction.

Section 7 Other Major Injuries to Human Health

Article 71 Burns and scalds.

(1) Total area of burns or scalds in adults exceeding thirty percent, or third-degree burns exceeding ten percent; total area in children exceeding ten percent, or third-degree burns exceeding five percent.

Burns or scalds with area below the above levels but with any of the following circumstances:

1. Shock;
2. Combined chemical poisoning;
3. Severe respiratory tract burns;
4. Complications leading to serious consequences; etc.

(2) Deep burns or scalds in special areas (such as the head, face, hands, perineum, etc.) severely affecting appearance and function; refer to relevant provisions on disfigurement of appearance, etc.

Article 72 Frostbite.

(1) Frostbite reaching third degree causing necrosis of the ears, nose, hands, feet, etc., and severe functional impairment.
(2) Frostbite causing local tissue defect, deformity, motor dysfunction, or chronic vascular pathology; etc.

Article 73 Disability of limbs after electric shock injury; with complications or severe sequelae.

Article 74 Physical injuries (such as radiation, laser, etc.), chemical injuries (such as strong acids, strong alkalis, etc.), or biological injuries (such as snake venom, pathogenic bacteria, etc.) causing severe dysfunction of internal organs or severe sequelae.

Article 75 Injury causing foreign body retention in important organs.

Article 76 Traumatic shock or injury complicated by severe infection causing dysfunction of the heart, liver, lungs, brain, kidneys, etc.

Article 77 Extensive subcutaneous hemorrhage with total area exceeding thirty percent, or intramuscular hemorrhage or hematoma exceeding ten percent, with complications or sequelae.

Article 78 Fat embolism syndrome caused by injury.

Article 79 Fracture of the jaw or injury to oral tissues (such as tongue defect) causing loss of speech ability, obvious impairment of chewing and swallowing functions.

Article 80 Injury to the eye region or craniocerebral injury causing diplopia that is difficult to recover, severely affecting work and daily life.

Chapter VII Supplementary Provisions

Article 81 In the case of multiple injuries, at least one injury must meet the criteria of these identification standards; different injuries shall not be aggregated to constitute a serious injury.

Article 82 These identification standards apply only to forensic medical identification of serious injuries as stipulated in the Criminal Law, and do not apply to specialized assessment of working capacity.

Article 83 The trial implementation period of these identification standards is from October 1, 1986, to September 30, 1988.

Explanation of the "Standards for Identification of Serious Injuries"

(1) Finger opposition activity refers to the action of the tip of the thumb meeting the tips of the other fingers. Normally, the tip of the thumb can oppose the tips of all other fingers.

(2) The area of the face refers to the region below the anterior hairline, between the anterior roots of both ears, and above the lower edge of the mandible, including the forehead, orbital region, nose, lips, chin, zygomatic region, cheeks, parotid-masseter region, and auricles.

(3) Methods for assessing hearing loss:

1. Hearing tests should preferably be conducted using an audiometer with air conduction as the standard. The unit for hearing level is the decibel (dB), and generally the average of three frequencies: 500, 1000, and 2000 Hertz is used. This average corresponds to the hearing threshold for conversational speech.

2. Hearing loss for speech not reaching 30 dB should be considered basically normal hearing.

3. After injury, hearing loss for speech in both ears is calculated by the following method:

(Hearing loss for speech in the better ear x 5 + Hearing loss for speech in the poorer ear x 1) divided by 6.

If the result shows hearing loss for speech at 60 dB or above, it should be considered a serious injury.

(4) Methods for assessing visual impairment:

1. Vision (referring to distance vision) that can be corrected to normal or near-normal with lenses is not considered visual impairment. Assessment of visual impairment should take "distance vision" as the standard, with reference to "near vision".

2. Central vision examination method: Use standard vision charts to test distance vision and near vision. After craniocerebral injury, central scotoma, physiological blind spot, and visual field examinations should be conducted. For cases with diplopia, a detailed examination and analysis of the nature of the diplopia should be performed.
